data.title: Trump's affinity for Putin harms US interests
data.description:
What is this thing President Trump has for Russian President Vladimir Putin — this respect for a brutal dictator and admiration for a war criminal? Why would an American president want to get so chummy with a man like Putin?   

On his way to a recent campaign rally, the president said, “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” before adding, “They haven’t been doing much.”

Words matter and in this case the president’s words are detached from reality. Russia has taken deliberate aim at civilians in Ukraine. Putin has targeted apartment buildings in Kyiv, the capital city. He’s aimed his missiles at hospitals and schools. And with winter approaching, he’s targeting what’s left of Ukraine’s electricity grid.

And yet the president tells us that “Russia has been fine on Ukraine,” and, “They haven’t been doing much.”

Maybe Trump thinks he can sweet-talk Putin to encourage him to make a deal to end the war. Or maybe that’s just wishful thinking. Maybe Trump’s affection for Putin is affecting his judgment?

For Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who’s fighting for his country’s very survival, Trump shows no respect, certainly no admiration. Instead, he shows contempt. 

“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine.” Trump says. “They’ve given nothing to us.”

So Trump has rolled out another red carpet for Putin — this time not literally as he did last summer in Alaska. This time the red carpet comes in the form of help from the president that would fuel Putin’s war machine and inflict more pain on Ukrainian civilians.

As David Sanger of the New York Times reports, Trump “shunted aside a bipartisan law, signed just weeks ago, imposing new tariffs on Russia. He cut a deal to purchase diesel from Moscow. His negotiators agreed on the vague outlines of a deal for much of Lukoil, a battered Russian energy firm.  And he called for the replacement of President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, whose success in taking the fight inside Russia deeply frustrates him.”

And just this week we learn that Russia has agreed to talks with Ukraine and the United States next month. But we shouldn’t expect much. The talks — if they even actually happen — would involve low-level representatives, and so there’s virtually no chance they would lead to an end to the war. 

Putin wants the kind of deal that Russia can live with and Ukraine can’t, the kind of deal he can persuade his “friend” President Trump to go along with and shove down Zelensky’s throat.

And at some point, it could happen — because the president blames Zelensky for keeping the war going, the war Russia started without provocation. He sees Ukraine, not Russia, as the obstacle to peace.

And while he was in Moscow this week, Steve Witkoff, the president’s chief negotiator, offered up a rhetorical kiss on the cheek to Vladimir Putin. The Russian president had just agreed to let a retired American teacher go free after being held for four years in a Russian prison.  

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff told Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

Let’s see if we have this right: Putin arrests an American on phony charges, convicts him in a Russian kangaroo court, keeps him locked up for four years, and when he releases him, he’s called a “humanitarian.” Maybe Putin also deserves a Nobel Peace Prize for his generosity.  

And while everyone was smiling and playing nice inside the Kremlin, while Trump’s man in Moscow was hailing Putin as a humanitarian, Russia was raining missiles on men, women and children inside Ukraine.  

And lost in all of this is another reality. It’s not only Ukraine that’s getting hammered. Our president’s “bromance” with Putin is also inflicting damage to America, to American values.

“President Trump and MAGA succeeded in part because they tapped into the sense of loss many Americans were feeling, the fear that the civilization the U.S. had helped create was in peril,” Gerry Baker writes in the Wall Street Journal. “They were elected to restore faith in America after years in which its leaders and culture had trashed American values.”

“America is still the greatest country on earth,” Baker goes on. “But its greatness will atrophy unless it restores its historic sense of purpose and the ideals of its founding principles and finds again leaders willing to place those ideals above the sordid, shameful, soul-defiling lust for power and money.”

Trump likes the company of strong, authoritarian men. That’s how he sees Putin. As far as Trump is concerned, Zelensky is a little obstinate man standing in the way of a deal that would not only end the killing, but also might get Trump the Nobel Peace Prize he believes he deserves.

So let me end where I began: What’s this thing President Trump has for Putin, a man who is following in the footsteps of Josef Stalin? Whatever this thing is, it’s not good for Ukraine — and it’s certainly not good for the United States of America. 

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page.

data.title: Norman's son says he's 'leaning' toward voting for Andrews for South Carolina Senate
data.description:
The son of GOP Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.), Warren Norman, said Friday he is “leaning” toward supporting the Democratic candidate in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews. 

Ralph Norman, who was defeated by Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in the GOP primary, said in a radio interview this week he would back the Republican nominee in the November election but indicated that his family would not vote for her. 

The Republican’s son made it official in an op-ed published in South Carolina outlet FITSNews, titled “Why This Lifelong Conservative Won’t Vote for Darline Graham.”

Warren Norman noted in his piece that the decision was not “personal,” extending his sympathy to Graham following the loss of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). 

However, he claimed that there was “no true conservative to vote for in this election.”

“If Senator Graham wins, the establishment that backed her will protect her in every primary to come,” Warren Norman wrote. “This seat could be hers for 24 years or more. 

“If Annie Andrews wins and doesn’t stand up to her party the way she has promised, South Carolina voters can hold her accountable and replace her with a strong conservative in six,” he continued. “Six years we can hold accountable, or 24 years we can’t. To me, that isn’t a hard call.” 

The Republican lawmaker’s son indicated that he was considering a vote for the Democratic nominee in the race instead. Despite disagreeing with Andrews “a lot,” the real estate partner said they agree “on some important things,” like opposing corruption and insurance reform.

“She struck me as genuine, and she has said publicly that she’ll stand up to her own party,” Warren Norman wrote. “That is the standard I’m asking of every candidate, and I intend to hold her to it. 

“As of today, I’m leaning her way,” he continued. “It will be the first time in my life I’ve voted for a Democrat in a partisan election.”

Andrews responded to Warren Norman’s op-ed in a statement to The Hill on Friday.

“South Carolinians deserve a senator who earns their vote, not someone handpicked by the same Washington insiders driving up our costs,” the Democratic candidate said. “Whether you voted for Donald Trump, Lindsey Graham, or anyone else, if you care more about lowering your bills than the political games in Washington, this campaign is for you. 

The Hill has reached out to Graham’s campaign for comment.

data.title: America's health insurance model crumbles under the success of modern medicine
data.description:
Every fall, millions of Americans sit down for the same grim ritual: open enrollment. The insurance logos are familiar, and the email from HR still insists the company is “committed to offering competitive benefits.” Then the sticker shock sets in. 

Heading into 2027, employer plan costs are projected to jump 9.5 percent, pushing the average past $19,000 per worker. On the Affordable Care Act marketplaces, insurers have proposed a median premium hike of 15 percent. And for millions buying their own coverage, the math has stopped working altogether. Over the last year, individual market enrollment plunged by more than 4.5 million people — dropping 18 percent from 25.2 million in 2025 to 20.5 million in mid-2026. Driven by the expiration of COVID-era enhanced tax credits and recent federal policy shifts, it is the steepest drop in a decade.

When premiums spike and millions lose coverage, it is easy to blame insurers, hospital monopolies or drugmakers. They bear plenty of responsibility. But the deeper failure is structural: Our health insurance model is an artifact of an era when medicine didn’t actually work very well.

Tying health insurance to employment and paying for it with pre-tax dollars is an accidental byproduct of World War II wage controls. Back then, medical care was rudimentary. Outside of setting a bone or delivering a baby, you mostly went to the hospital to die. Because effective interventions were rare, pooling risk through the workplace to cover the occasional hospital stay made sense.

Eighty years later, medicine works remarkably well. We have targeted biologics, gene therapies, and revolutionary drugs like GLP-1s that fundamentally alter the trajectory of chronic disease. Millions of people can, and should, take these therapies for a lifetime to stay healthy. 

The catch is you cannot finance a lifetime of expensive maintenance therapies for half the population through an insurance mechanism built for rare, unpredictable accidents. Insurance works when a large group pays a little each month to protect against a catastrophe that hits an unlucky few. When almost everyone needs ongoing care to stay healthy, the traditional risk pool breaks.

As the system buckles under the weight of new treatments and provider consolidation, employers and insurers fall back on their only playbook: shifting costs onto workers. Deductibles climb so high that millions of Americans are insured on paper, yet avoid the doctor because they cannot afford the bill.

Fixing this demands structural reform. We must retire our obsolete employer-sponsored model and rebuild healthcare financing around two distinct pillars.  

First, we implement universal catastrophic protection. Insurance should go back to being actual insurance. Every American should have baseline catastrophic coverage — detached from employment — that protects families from the financial ruin of a cancer diagnosis, a major surgery, an intensive care unit stay, or a million-dollar gene therapy. 

Second, we need a transparent cash market for routine and preventive care. For everyday medicine — primary care, diagnostics and routine maintenance medications — we should remove the insurance middleman. Routing predictable care through third-party payers adds massive administrative bloat while hiding real prices behind opaque insurer-provider negotiations. 

When providers and drugmakers have to compete directly for consumer dollars, prices fall fast. Look at what has happened with GLP-1s. While insurers scrambled to restrict coverage and employers balked at the cost, a direct-to-consumer cash market emerged. Over the last two years, fierce competition for cash-paying patients has driven the price of GLP-1 treatments down from more than $1,500 a month to starting prices around $150 a month. 

That is what happens when incentives align. Transparent competition replaces bureaucratic rationing, and care actually becomes affordable.

To accelerate this transition, policymakers should stop funneling hundreds of billions of dollars in pre-tax subsidies exclusively into bloated, employer-chosen plans. Instead, tax advantages should go directly to individuals to pair portable catastrophic coverage with flexible accounts they can spend on routine, preventive cash-pay care. In the near term, lawmakers should also mandate that whenever a patient pays cash for a service at or below their insurer’s negotiated rate, that spending must count toward their annual deductible. 

We are trying to pay for 21st-century medical miracles with a mid-20th-century financing model. As 4.5 million Americans fall off the individual marketplaces and employer costs surge past $19,000 per worker, the cracks in the foundation are impossible to ignore. It is time to build universal protection for the medical catastrophes that could bankrupt us, and unleash transparent cash markets for the everyday care that keeps us healthy. 

Michael Botta is a healthcare economist and co-founder of Sesame.

data.title: Melania Trump brokers localized Russia-Ukraine ceasefire, White House says
data.description:
First Lady Melania Trump has secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the frontline city of Oleshky, the White House said in a press release Friday morning.

The ceasefire will begin Oct. 29 with both nations agreeing to temporarily stop all military action in the city “to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” the release said.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” the first lady said in the release.

“It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she added.

The Ukrainian embassy confirmed to The Hill that a ceasefire was reached for Oleshky.

On Tuesday, Ukraine’s embassy along with the Norwegian embassy co-hosted a briefing about the situation in Oleshky, the embassy posted on social platform X.

“Some 25,000 people lived in Oleshky before the full-scale invasion. About 2,000 remain, including 35 children. They have gone years without electricity, gas, heating, or running water,” the embassy wrote in the post. “No food has been officially delivered since May 26, 2026, and the only supply route runs through mined territory under shelling.”

In Friday’s release, the first lady said non-military, civilian leaders from both Ukraine and Russia will work together to visit the homes of residents in the war-torn city to determine the level of assistance required.

“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.

The city of Oleshky is located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson Oblast on the east bank of the Dnipro River. The city had a pre-war population of around 24,000 people and was pulled to the frontline after Ukraine liberated western Kherson Oblast in November 2022, according to a report from the Institute for the Study of War.

With much of its population displaced or evacuated, the city now has about 1,700-2,000 remaining residents, according to the White House release.

Laura Kelly contributed to this report.

data.title: Oil prices hit highest point since May
data.description:
Oil prices on Friday hit their highest point since May as the war in Iran drags on.

As of Friday morning, futures for international benchmark Brent Crude were trading at $116 per barrel, while U.S benchmark WTI traded at about $102.

The high prices come as the war in Iran is in its eighth month and shows no signs of stopping.

While vessels have been moving through the Strait of Hormuz, shipping in the Middle East has become increasingly expensive due to war-related risks.

Gasoline prices were also relatively high, but lower than they have been in recent weeks. As of Friday; the average U.S. price was about $4.29 per gallon according to AAA, down about 18 cents from a month ago but up about $1.22 from a year ago. 

If oil prices remain high, gas prices could go even higher as the midterms loom.

data.title: 2 Air Force pilots eject from training jet in Texas
data.description:
Two Air Force pilots safely ejected from their aircraft near San Antonio Thursday due to potential issues with their landing gear. 

The pilots —  who were part of a training program at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph in Texas — received indications their landing gear was unsafe and ejected at the recommendation of experts, a statement from the base said. The pilots were evaluated by local medical personnel.

“Two pilots successfully ejected from a T-6A Texan II assigned to the 12th Flying Training Wing during a controlled bailout near Seguin, Texas,” a release from the base states.

The 12th Flying Training Wing is a program that develops enlisted Air Force aviators and crew members through “flying training and education.” Airmen in the program are trained in a variety of disciplines including combat systems officer training, pilot instructor training and enlisted aviator training.

The sheriff’s office for nearby Wilson County said in a Thursday Facebook post that they were responding to the scene of an “aircraft accident” along with a number of other agencies. They affirmed that there was no threat to the public. 

“You can expect a large presence of law enforcement, military, fire, and EMS personnel,” the Wilson County Sheriff’s Office wrote at the time.

data.title: Trump election advisers donate Bosnia consulting fee to presidential library
data.description:
President Trump’s political advisers James Blair and Chris LaCivita confirmed on Friday that they donated their full fee from their consulting work for a pro-Russian political party in Bosnia to Trump’s presidential library. 

“Yes, it’s true we donated our full fee. I love the President and am eternally grateful for the opportunities he has provided me,” Blair said in a post on X, referring to the New York Post story which was first to report on the donation. 

“Contributing to the preservation of his legacy of greatness is my honor!” Blair said. 

LaCivita reposted Blair, writing “preserving the legacy and story of @realDonaldTrump is an honor and a no brainer!” 

The Trump Presidential Library and Museum is expected to be housed in Miami, Fla. 

The donations come after Trump warned earlier this month that he would terminate Blair and LaCivita if their work in the Balkans conflicted with the White House. 

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them.”

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” he continued. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

data.title: Make universities limit ties to China — and fund US STEM students instead
data.description:
The War Department announcement that thirty universities have “fully mitigated” their relationships with “foreign entities of concern” — most notably Chinese academic institutions — is a welcome development. These “entities” appear on the latest update to the list mandated by the 2019 National Defense Authorization Act to identify “foreign institutions engaging in problematic activities.”

The department’s latest update of the list identified 130 such institutions “located in China, Russia and Iran” whose activities enable “adversarial government interference.”

Not surprisingly, the department’s latest announcement has met some skepticism if not outright opposition from some of the thirty universities that have agreed to mitigation. Several have announced that they will not cut all ties with China; after all, “mitigated” is not the same as “terminated.”

The universities’ reaction should come as no surprise. For years, American institutions of higher learning and their supporters have argued that cooperation with their foreign counterparts is critical to advancing cutting-edge research. As a 2025 letter from the Asian American Scholar Forum to the chairmen and ranking members of the Armed Services Committees put it, “critical to our research enterprise is our ability to attract and retain the best global talents, foster international collaborations, and reduce the chilling effect on the Asian American and broader research community.”

This has been especially true with respect to the longstanding debate over restricting the number of Chinese students attending U.S. universities — an issue over which the American public is evenly divided. In fact, the number of Chinese students attending American universities declined during the past decade from a peak of 370,000 in 2018 to 266,000 in the 2024-2025 academic year. But that is still a significant number.

As Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chairman of the House Select Committee on China, outlined in a recent letter to Secretary Pete Hegseth, many Chinese students receive their support—and can pay full tuition — from the China Scholarship Council, which targets “STEM disciplines aligned with China’s industrial policies and medium to long-term development plans [and is] a key channel for transferring human talent, intellectual capital, and technical expertise back to [China] in support of its national strategic objectives.”

Moreover, Moolenaar notes, the council requires sponsored students to submit regular reports to Chinese authorities “detailing their academic progress, laboratory work, research outputs and publications,” to return to China after competing their studies, and to serve in government afterward for at least two years.

For these reasons, Moolenaar demands that the War Department “prohibit any researcher, graduate student, postdoctoral researcher or other research personnel receiving funding or financial support from the China Scholarship Council from participating” in research funded by the department. This would no doubt result in a further decline in the number of Chinese students attending American institutions of higher learning.

Those who oppose such restrictions go so far as to claim that “banning Chinese students would cast the strategic competition with China as a racially motivated action … banning an entire group of citizens from Asia would not only light a match under our relations with China, it would also outrage several of our close allies around the region.”

But Moolenaar’s letter does not call for a ban on all Chinese students, nor is the argument for reducing their number racially motivated. On the contrary, there is much to be said for welcoming foreign researchers, whatever their race, to study in the U.S. and collaborate with, American university programs — especially those related to cutting-edge technologies. As a member of the Congressionally mandated National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, I have met throughout the U.S. with leading researchers who have made breakthroughs on the most advanced biotechnology projects; many of them are non-white first-generation Americans.

The U.S. must continue to attract the most talented foreign academics and researchers if it is to remain the world’s leading source of technological innovation. But it cannot open its doors to students who have direct links to the Chinese government and the Chinese Communist Party. That would contribute to Beijing’s tireless effort to replace the U.S. as the world’s technological leader.

Instead, as I suggested five years ago, the Pentagon should set aside funds to expand its scholarship programs for students who until now could not attend the university programs of their choice because they could not afford to pay for them and were displaced by Chinese students who could.

In that way, not only would the War Department prevent Beijing’s exploitation of our intellectual resources, but by supporting an expanded pool of talented young Americans hoping to pursue careers in advanced technology, it also would further strengthen the nation’s intellectual and technological security.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was under secretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy under secretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Manchin: Collins should leave GOP, become an independent
data.description:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) suggested this week that Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) should leave the Republican Party to become an independent. 

Manchin, who made the switch from the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024, has repeatedly pushed for more lawmakers to break away from the two-party system. 

The former senator told Semafor after joining the Maine incumbent on the campaign trail this week that Collins “is independent” but that she “has to come to that conclusion” first.

“She’s as independent as any Republican is up there,” Manchin told the outlet. “But the bottom line is, she has to make that decision.”

The Hill has reached out to the Maine senator’s campaign for comment. 

Manchin visited a New Balance shoe factory in southwestern Maine for a campaign stop with Collins this week, after endorsing her reelection bid in September.

The senator has built a reputation in Congress as a moderate Republican, breaking with her party on key votes like an April Iran war powers resolution. 

She also voted to convict President Trump in his second impeachment trial in 2021 and opposed repealing the Affordable Care Act in 2017. 

Collins is seeking a sixth term in the Senate in a closely watched reelection race in the Pine Tree State against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson. 

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates this race as a “toss up.” A Fox News poll released on Thursday showed the two candidates tied up at 49 percent. Recent polling from Suffolk University and Marist University have shown Jackson posting moderate leads over the incumbent senator that fall within the surveys’ margins of error. 

Manchin also told Semafor that he is working with The Independent Leadership Council, which he co-founded in July, to support candidates running in Montana, Idaho and Nebraska. The group aims to elect more independent leaders to Congress.

data.title: Cook Political Report shifts 19 House seats in Democrats' favor
data.description:
Nonpartisan election forecaster Cook Political Report has shifted 19 House seats in Democrats’ direction less than two weeks before the midterm elections, according to its latest report published Friday.

The shift includes six seats held by Republicans that were previously noted as a “Toss Up” and have now been changed to “Lean Democrat”: Reps. Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Gabe Evans (Colo.), Jen Kiggans (Va.) and Derrick Van Orden (Wis.).

“Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House,” Cook Political Report’s U.S. House of Representatives editor Erin Covey wrote in the report. “Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican. That leaves 17 races rated as pure Toss Ups.”

Two open seats — in Kentucky’s 6th and Texas’s 35th congressional districts — have been moved from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up,” according to Cook’s predictions. In the Lexington, Ky.-based district, Democrat Zach Dembo is facing Republican Ralph Alvarado. In the San Antonio district, Democrat Johnny Garcia is going up against Republican Carlos De La Cruz.

Per Cook’s analysis, the “likeliest outcome” is “Democrats flipping between 12 and 22 seats.” According to the projections, Democrats will hold anywhere between 227 to 237 seats next year, while Republicans are projected to hold between 208 and 198 seats.

Cook’s analysis comes as President Trump’s approval ratings hit new lows in the latest polls from The New York Times/Siena University and CNN in the final stretch of the upcoming midterm elections. The Times reported Tuesday that the president’s 36 percent approval was a record low for all Times/Siena polls.

Trump’s approval rating in the CNN poll stood at 32 percent, also a historic low as reported by the outlet Tuesday, with voters expressing broad dissatisfaction with both the economy and the state of the country.
